terms.definition: A slow tempo marking, typically between 66-76 BPM.
terms.example: Play this passage adagio for a more expressive interpretation.

terms.definition: A fast, lively tempo marking, typically between 120-168 BPM.
terms.example: The first movement is marked allegro.

terms.definition: A moderate walking tempo, typically between 76-108 BPM.
terms.example: The second movement should be played andante.

terms.definition: A very slow, broad tempo marking, typically 40-60 BPM.
terms.example: The opening is marked largo for dramatic effect.

terms.definition: A very fast tempo marking, typically 168-200 BPM.
terms.example: The finale is presto, requiring great technical skill.

terms.definition: A lively, brisk tempo marking, typically 132-168 BPM.
terms.example: Play this section vivace to convey excitement.

terms.definition: A moderate tempo marking, typically 108-120 BPM.
terms.example: The piece begins moderato before accelerating.

terms.definition: A slow tempo marking, slower than adagio, typically 40-60 BPM.
terms.example: The lento section creates a contemplative mood.

terms.definition: A gradual increase in volume or intensity.
terms.example: Build a crescendo from piano to forte.

terms.definition: A gradual decrease in volume or intensity. Also called diminuendo.
terms.example: The decrescendo fades the music to silence.

terms.definition: A gradual decrease in volume or intensity. Same as decrescendo.
terms.example: Apply a diminuendo at the end of the phrase.

terms.definition: Play loudly, abbreviated as 'f'.
terms.example: The chorus enters forte.

terms.definition: Pianoforte - "Soft-loud." A keyboard instrument, the full name for the piano, on which sound is produced by hammers striking strings when keys are pressed. It has 88 keys.
terms.example: The introduction is marked piano.

terms.definition: Moderately loud, abbreviated as 'mf'.
terms.example: The main theme is mezzo forte.

terms.definition: Moderately soft, abbreviated as 'mp'.
terms.example: The accompaniment should be mezzo piano.

terms.definition: Very loud, abbreviated as 'ff'.
terms.example: The climax is fortissimo.

terms.definition: Very, very soft; the softest common dynamic marking.
terms.example: The ending fades to pianissimo.

terms.definition: Detached sounds, indicated by a dot over or under a note. The opposite of legato.
terms.example: The staccato notes create a light, bouncy effect.

terms.definition: Play notes smoothly connected, indicated by a slur.
terms.example: The melody should be played legato.

terms.definition: Play notes with emphasis, marked with a wedge-shaped accent.
terms.example: The marcato notes add rhythmic drive.

terms.definition: Hold the note for its full value, indicated by a horizontal line.
terms.example: Each note should be tenuto for maximum expression.

terms.definition: > placed above a note to indicate stress or emphasis.
terms.example: The accented notes mark the downbeat.

terms.definition: Hold the note longer than its written value, indicated by a curved symbol.
terms.example: Hold the fermata for dramatic effect.

terms.definition: Rapid alternation between two adjacent notes.
terms.example: The trill adds ornamentation to the melody.

terms.definition: "Biting." An ornament consisting of an alteration (once or twice) of the written note by playing the one immediately below it (lower mordent), or above it (upper, or inverted, mordent) and then playing the note again.
terms.example: The mordent decorates the principal note.

terms.definition: A musical ornament characterized by the rapid performance of a given note, the major or minor second above and below, and a return to the given note.
terms.example: The turn adds elegance to the phrase.

terms.definition: A nonharmonic tone, usually a half or whole step above the harmonic tone, which is performed on the beat and then resolved.
terms.example: The appoggiatura creates tension before resolution.

terms.definition: A symbol placed at the beginning of the staff to indicate the pitch of the notes on the staff. The most commonly used clefs in choral music are the G, or treble, clef and the F or bass clef. On the keyboard, all the notes above middle C are said to be in the G clef; all the notes below middle C in the F clef.
terms.example: The treble clef is used for higher-pitched instruments.

terms.definition: Also called G clef, indicates that the second line from the bottom is G above middle C.
terms.example: Violin and flute parts use the treble clef.

terms.definition: Also called F clef, indicates that the fourth line from the bottom is F below middle C.
terms.example: Bass and cello parts use the bass clef.

terms.definition: Indicates the meter of the music, showing beats per measure and note value.
terms.example: 4/4 time means four quarter notes per measure.

terms.definition: The sharps or flats placed at the beginning of the staff to denote the scale upon which the music is based.
terms.example: Three sharps indicate the key of A major.

terms.definition: # A symbol which raises the pitch of a note one-half step.
terms.example: F sharp is one semitone higher than F.

terms.definition: ♭ A symbol which lowers the pitch of a note one half step.
terms.example: B flat is one semitone lower than B.

terms.definition: Cancels a sharp or flat, returning the note to its natural pitch.
terms.example: The natural sign cancels the previous sharp.

terms.definition: A curved line over or below two or more notes of the same pitch. The first pitch is sung or played and held for the duration of the notes affected by the tie.
terms.example: The tie extends the note's duration.

terms.definition: A curved line placed above or below two or more notes of different pitch to indicate that they are to be performed in legato style.
terms.example: Notes under a slur should be played smoothly.

terms.definition: A group of beats containing a primary accent and one or more secondary accents, indicated by the placement of bar lines on the staff. The space between two bar lines.
terms.example: Each measure contains four beats in 4/4 time.

terms.definition: The vertical line placed on the staff to divide the music into measures.
terms.example: The bar line marks the end of each measure.

terms.definition: Indicates that a section of music should be played again.
terms.example: The repeat sign means play the section twice.

terms.definition: Abbreviated as D.C., means 'from the beginning'.
terms.example: After the trio, return da capo.

terms.definition: Abbreviated as D.S., means 'from the sign'.
terms.example: Dal segno directs you to return to the sign.

terms.definition: Closing section of a composition. An added ending.
terms.example: Jump to the coda after the D.S. marking.

terms.definition: A succession of tones. The scale generally used in Western music is the diatonic scale, consisting of whole and half steps in a specific order.
terms.example: Practice the major scale daily.

terms.definition: A combination of three or more tones sounded simultaneously.
terms.example: The C major chord consists of C, E, and G.

terms.definition: The difference in pitch between two tones.
terms.example: A perfect fifth spans five scale degrees.

terms.definition: The sounding of two or more tones simultaneously; the vertical aspect of music.
terms.example: The harmony supports the melody.

terms.definition: In general, a succession of musical tones. It represents the linear or horizontal aspect of music.
terms.example: The melody is memorable and singable.

terms.definition: The term which denotes the organization of sound in time; the temporal quality of sound.
terms.example: The rhythm drives the piece forward.

terms.definition: The basic unit of time in music, the pulse you tap your foot to.
terms.example: Keep a steady beat throughout.

terms.definition: The speed at which a piece of music is played.
terms.example: The tempo marking indicates the speed.

terms.definition: The structure of notes in a regular pattern of accented and unaccented beats within a measure, indicated at the beginning of a composition by a meter signature.
terms.example: The meter determines the strong and weak beats.

terms.definition: The first beat of a measure, usually the strongest.
terms.example: Emphasize the downbeat for clarity.

terms.definition: One or more notes occurring before the first bar line, as necessitated by the text for the purpose of desirable accent. The unaccented beat of a measure.
terms.example: The upbeat prepares the next measure.

terms.definition: Accenting beats that are normally weak, creating rhythmic interest.
terms.example: The syncopation creates a sense of forward motion.

terms.definition: A chordal or melodic progression which occurs at the close of a phrase, section, or composition, giving a feeling of repose; a temporary or permanent ending. The most frequently used cadences are perfect, plagal, and deceptive.
terms.example: The perfect cadence provides a strong ending.

terms.definition: A relatively short portion of a melodic line which expresses a musical idea, comparable to a line or sentence in poetry.
terms.example: Each phrase should be shaped expressively.

terms.definition: A short musical idea that recurs throughout a piece.
terms.example: The opening motif appears throughout the symphony.

terms.definition: The musical subject of a piece (usually a melody), as in sonata form or a fugue. An extramusical concept behind a piece.
terms.example: The main theme is introduced in the exposition.

terms.definition: The manipulation of a theme by the use of melodic, rhythmic, and harmonic changes.
terms.example: Each variation explores different aspects of the theme.

terms.definition: The process of changing the key of a composition.
terms.example: The piece was transposed from C major to D major.

terms.definition: The process of changing from one key to another within a composition.
terms.example: The modulation to the dominant key creates tension.

terms.definition: Intervallic relationships which produce sounds of repose. Frequently associated with octave, third and sixth intervals; however, fourths and fifths may be sounds of consonance, as in both early and 20th-century music.
terms.example: Perfect fifths create consonance.

terms.definition: Sounds of unrest, e.g. intervals of seconds and sevenths; the opposite of consonance.
terms.example: The dissonance creates tension before resolution.

terms.definition: Absolute music. Music which is inspired by itself rather than extramusical implications such as the stories legends of "program" music.
Gradually faster.
A sharp, flat, or natural not included in the given key.
A vocal or instrument part that supports or is background for a solo part.
Sorrowfully.
A term which permits the performer to vary the tempo and/or to include or omit a vocal or instrumental part. Synonymous with a piacere.
Return to unison after divisi.
Hurrying.
Lively.
Agitated; with excitement.
To; used with other words, e.g. al Fine (to the end).
A full length recording. In pop music, it contains a number of songs.
"To the coda."
Chance music in which the performers are free to perform their own material and/or their own manner of presentation.
To the end.
meter in which there are two beats in each measure and a half note receives one beat.
Slowing of tempo, usually with increasing volume; most frequently occurs toward the end of a piece.
Slower than allegro.
Return to the sign, Dal segno.
The raising or lowering of a note by means of an accidental.
The C clef falling on the third line of the staff. Most of the time is used by the viola.
Repeat.
Slightly faster than andante.
To nothing, e.g. to ppp.
Animated; lively.
Freedom in performance. Synonymous with ad libitum.
Impassioned.
A fanciful piano piece. Ornate passage varying or accompanying a theme.
A term used to describe the pitches of a chord as they are sung or played one after the other, rather than simultaneously.
Strong pizzicato.
An adaption of a composition.
The degree to which notes are separated or connected, such as staccato or legato. A tempo - Return to the previous tempo.
Lacking a tonal center.
Compositional technique in which a melodic line is repeated in longer note values. The opposite of diminution.
A small grand piano.
The harmonious adjustment of volume and timbre between instruments or voices; it can be between players or vocalists or electronically while recording or mixing.

The term for a major or perfect interval which has been enlarged by one half-step, e.g. c-g #, (an augmented fifth,) or c-d, (an augmented second). Also used for a triad with an augmented fifth, e.g. the augmented tonic triad in C major, C+, c-e-g.
In the medieval period a form of trouvere music and poetry. In later time, German poetry set as a through-composed song.
An instrumental ensemble, usually made up of wind and percussion instruments and no string instruments.
The period 1600-1750.
bass - The Baroque practice in which the bass part if played by a viola da gamba (cello) or bassoon while a keyboard instrument performed the bass line and the indicated chords.
Conductor's stick.
Beat, bar, or measure. A due or a tre battuta, the musical rhythm in groups of two or three respectively.
Well. Used with other words, e.g. ben marcato, well accented, emphasized.
The term for describing a composition of two sections. AB, each of which may be repeated.
Repeated twice. Encore!
The occurrence of two different tonalities at the same time.
A French dance from the 17th century in brisk duple time starting with a pickup.
Wind instruments made out of metal with either a cup- or funnel-shaped mouthpiece, such as trumpet, cornet, bugle, Flugelhorn, trombone, tuba, baritone horn, euphonium, saxhorn, and French horn.
Notes of a chord played in succession rather than simultaneously. Arpeggio.
a solo passage, often virtuosic, usually near the end of a piece, either written by the composer or improvised by the performer.
A sudden silencing of the sound; a pause or break, indicated by the following symbol: //
Calm.
A direction found in scores to change tuning or instruments.
Following easily and gently.
The strictest form of imitation, in which two or more parts have the same melody but start at different points.
A term used to describe a polyphonic style of music in which all the parts have the same melody but which start at different times.
In singing style.
Baroque sacred or secular choral composition containing solos, duets, and choruses, with orchestral or keyboard accompaniment.

The term was derived from a medieval French word, carole, a circle dance. In England it was first associated with pagan songs celebrating the winter solstice. It then developed into a song of praise and celebration, usually for Christmas.

A clef usually centered on the first line (soprano clef), third line (alto clef), fourth line (tenor clef), or third space (vocal tenor clef) of the staff. Wherever it is centered, that line or space becomes middle C.
Aleatoric music.
Hymn-like song, characterized by blocked chords.
Ascending or descending by half steps.
A scale composed of 12 half steps.
The succession of keys or chords proceeding by fifths.
Music conforming to certain form and structure. Usually music composed during the period 1770-1825.
With or "with the."
4/4 meter.
I-IV-V-I progression.
A person who creates (composes) music.
With.
With spirit; vigorously.
With warmth.
A public performance of music.
The largest of the grand pianos, usually about nine feet long.
A short concerto. The group of soloists in a concerto grosso.
First chair violinist in an orchestra.
A piece for a soloist and orchestra.
The international tuning pitch -- currently A 440 or 442. The pitch for non-transposing (C) instruments.
The directing of a group of musicians.
The person who directs a group of musicians.
With intensity.
Pitches on successive degrees of the scale; opposite of disjunct.
With motion.
A 17th-century term for instrumental chamber ensembles and for the compositions written for these ensembles.
With spirit.
The octave below normal.
String.
A vocal part which contrasts with the principal melody.
The technique of combining single melodic lines or parts of equal importance.
Indication by the conductor or a spoken word or gesture for a performer to make an entry. Small notes that indicate another performer's part. Music occurrence in a film.
2/2 meter.
Repeat from the sign. Frequently followed by al Fine.
On pianos, the pedal that lifts the dampers from the strings.
Chordal progression dominant (V) to a chord other than the expected tonic.
One of the eight consecutive tones in a major or minor scale.
Delicately.
Of, with.

The term for an interval which has been decreased from the major by two half steps and from the perfect by one half step, e.g. c-a, diminished sixth, or c-g ♭♭ , a diminished fifth. Also used for a triad which has a minor third and a diminished fifth, e.g. c, c-e♭, g♭.
Gradually softer. Synonymous with decrescendo.
The shortening of note values; the opposite of augmentation.
A piece that is performed at a funeral or memorial service.
The term used to describe intervals larger than a second; the opposite of conjunct.
An indication of divided musical parts.
The first degree of the major scale.
Sweetly.
Very sweetly.
Sadly; mournfully.
The fifth degree of the major or minor scale. Also, the term for the triad built on the fifth degree, labelled V in harmonic analysis.
Two vertical lines placed on the staff to indicate the end of a section or a composition. Also, used with two dots to enclose repeated sections.
♭♭ A symbol for lowering pitch one step.
𝄪 A symbol for raising pitch one step.
On flute and brass instruments, the technique of rapidly articulating notes by using the front and the back of the tongue in alternation (t-k-t-k-t-k).
The first beat; given by the conductor with a downward stroke.
In the violin family, drawing the bow downward from its frog. The symbol is: Du - "From the," "of the."
A piece for two performers.
A group of two notes performed in the time of three of the same kind.
Varying degrees of loud and soft.
Italian word meaning "and."
Octave.
A note/rest half the length of a quarter note and an eighth of the length of a whole note.
To repeat a piece or play an additional piece at the end of a performance.
A term used to describe notes of the same pitch which have different names, e.g. c♯ and d♭, f♭ and g.
Expressively.
Exuberant.
In solmization, the fourth degree of the major scale.
A prelude or opening, a flourish, usually played by brass instruments.
A system of solmization used in 17th- and 18th-century England and America. Fa, so, and la were given to both c-d-e and f-g-a, with mi used for the seventh degree.
Festive; merry.

The fifth degree of the diatonic scale. Also, the interval formed by a given tone and the fifth tone above or below it, e.g. c up to g, c down to f. Intervals of the fifth may be perfect (corresponding to major), diminished, or augmented.
The last movement of a symphony or sonata, or the last selection of an opera.
The end.
One or more measures which occur at the end of the stanza or stanzas. It is usually indicated:
The system of solmization in which c is always do.
The design or structure of a musical composition.
An instrumental score in which all the parts for the instruments appear on their own staves in standard instrumental family order.

The fourth degree of the diatonic scale. Also, the interval formed by a given tone and the fourth tone above or below it, e.g. c up to f; c down to g. Intervals of the fourth may be perfect, diminished, or augmented.
Forzando or forzato. Synonymous with sforzando (sf or sfz).
A job for a musician.
Playful.
Exultant, jubilant.

Gliss. The rapid scale achieved by sliding the nail of the thumb or third finger over the white keys of the piano. Glissando is commonly used in playing the harp. For bowed instruments glissando indicates a flowing, unaccented playing of a passage.
Grandiose, majestic.
A rest for the entire ensemble.
A piano with a winglike shape and a horizontal frame, strings, and soundboard.
The G and F clef staves together make the grand (great) staff.
Slow, solemn.
Grace. Con grazia, with grace.
Graceful.
Great, large.
The interval from one pitch to the immediately adjacent pitch, ascending or descending, e.g. c-c♯; e-e♭; b-c. The smallest interval on the keyboard.
The term applied to time values in the ration of 3:2, e.g. three half notes in place of two dotted half notes.
Musical texture which is characterized by chordal support of a melodic line.
A musical movement of the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Inspired by the French impressionist painters, the movement had its impetus in the music of Debussy and Ravel.
Any device that produces a musical sound.
The art of composing, orchestrating, or arranging for an instrumental ensemble. Also, the collection of instruments required for a specific ensemble or musical selection.

As applied to music the term may be used in both melody and harmony. Melodic inversion: an exchange of ascending and descending movement, e.g. c up to f in descending becomes c down to g. Harmonic inversion: the position of the chord is changed from root position (root on the lowest pitch) to first inversion, with the third, or second inversion, with the fifth in the lowest voice. An example: root position c-e-g; first inversion e-g-c; second inversion g-c-е.
Ironical.

In solmization, the sixth degree of the major scale. Also, the first degree of the relative minor scale, e.g. a is the sixth degree, or la, in the C major scale and the first degree of the a-minor scale.
Tearful, mournful.
Mournful, sad.
Slow.
Broadly.
Slower than largo.
The seventh degree of the major scale, so called because of its strong tendency to resolve upward to the tonic.
Short lines placed above and below the staff for pitches beyond the range of the staff.
Light; graceful.
Freely.
Melodic; horizontal lines.
But. Used with other words, e.g. lento ma non troppo, slow but not too slowly.
Majestically.

The designation for certain intervals and scales. A key based on a major scale is called a major key. The pattern of whole and half steps for the major scale is: whole whole half whole whole whole half
A triad composed of a root, major third, and perfect fifth.
Fading away.
The same.
The third degree of the major or minor scale. The triad built on this degree is labeled iii in the major scale, III in the natural minor scale, and III in the harmonic minor scale.
The period prior to the Renaissance, c. 500-1450, marking the music of the early Christian church.
Less.
Less motion.

The numbers placed at the beginning of a composition to indicate the meter of the music, e.g.. The upper number indicates the beats in a measure; the lower number tells what kind of a note will receive one beat.

Invented by Maelzel in 1816, the instrument is used to indicate the exact tempo of a composition. An indication such as M.M. 60 indicates that the pendulum, with a weight at the bottom, makes 60 beats per minute. A slider is moved up and down the pendulum to decrease and increase the tempo. M.M. = 80 means that the time value of a quarter note is the equivalent of one pendulum beat when the slider is set at 80.
Half, Medium
In solmization, the third degree of the major scale.
European historical period between roughly A.D. 500 and 1450.
The note C in the middle of the Grand staff, and near the middle of the piano.
The designation for certain intervals and scales. A key based on a minor scale is called a minor
Mysteriously
with (German)

Any scalewise arrangement of pitches; more generally, the term refers to the patterns upon which medieval music was structured, the patterns which preceded the development of major and minor scales and tonality.
Music written in the 20th century or contemporary music.
Very. Used with other terms, e.g. molto allegro.
Gradually decreasing in volume; dying away.
Rapid. Meno mosso, less rapid. Piu mosso, more rapid.
A short melodic or rhythmic pattern.
Motion. Con moto, with motion.

The system of solmization in which do changes to accommodate the key, e.g. in the key of C major, do is c; in E major do is e. In the key of a minor do is c (relative major); in the key of c minor do is e (relative major).
The organization of sounds with some degree of rhythm, melody, and harmony.
The study of how music is put together.
After (as "in the manner of"); behind.
"Night music." A serenade.
One style of chant in which two to four pitches occur on one syllable; in contrast to melismatic and syllabic.
No; not.
A designation for tones outside the harmonic structure of the chord. Two frequently used examples are the passing tone and the appoggiatura.
Not too much. Used with other terms, e.g. non troppo allegro, not too fast.
A term for a system of expressing musical sounds through the use of written characters, called notes.
The symbol which, when placed on a staff with a particular clef sign, indicates pitch.
Subtle variations in tempo, phrasing, dynamics, etc., to enhance a musical performance.
The eighth tone above a given pitch, with twice as many vibrations per second, or below a given pitch, with half as many vibrations.
A piece for eight instruments or voices.
A triad without a third.
Strings are not stopped, fingered, or fretted.
The term, meaning work, is used by composers to show the chronological order of their works, e.g. Op. 1, Op. 2.
A large group of musicians made up of string, brass, woodwind, and percussion instruments.
The art of writing, arranging, or scoring for the orchestra.
Note or notes added to the original melodic line for embellishment and added interest.
Melodic embellishments, either written or improvised.
"Or." Indicating an alternative passage or version.
A repeated melodic or rhythmic pattern, frequently appearing in the bass line.
Octave.
(8va) An octave higher.
(8va or 8vb) An octave lower.

The almost inaudible higher tones which occur with the fundamental tone. They are the result of the vibration of small sections of a string (instrument) or a column of air. Other general terms for overtones are partials and harmonics.
The introductory music for an opera, oratorio or ballet. A concert overture is an independent work.
Calm, quiet.
Unaccented notes which move conjunctly between two chords to which they do not belong harmonically.
A rest.
Contemplative, thoughtful.
Instruments made of sonorous material that produce sounds of definite or indefinite pitch when shaken or struck, including drums, rattles, bells, gongs, and xylophones.
A term used to label fourth, fifth, and octave intervals. It corresponds to the major, as given to seconds, thirds, sixths, and sevenths.
The chordal progression of dominant to tonic, in a major key V-I, in minor V-i.
Interval of an octave, fifth, or fourth without alteration.
The ability to hear and identify a note without any other musical support.
Heavy.
Little.
Little by little.
The term for the raising of the third, making a major triad, in the final chord of a composition which is in a minor key. The practice originated in c. 1500 and extended through the Baroque period.
The highness or lowness of a tone, as determined by the number of vibrations in the sound.
More. Used with other terms, e.g. piu mosso, more motion.
"Pinched." On string instruments, plucking the string.
Sometimes called the "amen" cadence. The chordal progression of subdominant to tonic, in a major key IV-I, in minor iv-i.
Little. Used with other terms, e.g. poco accel., also, poco a poco, little by little.
A little slower.
A little more motion.
Then or afterwards, e.g. poi No. 3, then No. 3.
"Play after." The final piece in a multi-movement work. Organ piece played at the end of a church service.
"Play before." An introductory movement or piece.
First performance.
Very, very fast. The fastest tempo.
First.
Instrumental section leader.
An introductory piece that presents the background for an opera.
A note/rest one half the length of a half note and one quarter the length of a whole note.
A piece for four instruments or voices. Four performers.
Almost. Used with other terms, e.g. quasi madrigal, almost or as if a madrigal.
A piece for five instruments or voices. Five performers.
Gradually slower. Synonymous with ritardando.
The gamut of pitches, from low to high, which a singer may perform.
Rapidly.
In solmization, the second degree of the major scale.
A performance by one or more performers.
A short section of repeated material which occurs at the end of each stanza.
Major and minor scales which have the same key signature.
The period c. 1450-1600.
The repetition of a section or a composition as indicated by particular signs. Repeat of a section: Repeat from the beginning: Also D.C., repeat from the beginning and D.S., repeat from the sign.
Reinforcement and intensification of sound by vibrations.
A symbol used to denote silence.
A free style instrumental piece characterized by dramatic changes in mood.
A reinforced accent.
Resolute.
Gradually slower. Synonymous with rallentando.
Immediate reduction in tempo.
Rhythmically.
On percussion instruments, a sticking technique consisting of a rapid succession of notes.
The period c. 1825-1900.
The note upon which a triad or chord is built.
The arrangement of a chord in which the root is in the lowest voice.
Like the canon, a song in which two or more parts having the same melody, starting at different points. The parts may be repeated as desired.
The term used to denote flexibility of tempo to assist in achieving expressiveness.
On drums, the basic sticking patterns.
Quiet.
A rapid scale passage.
Pastoral, rustic, rural.
Soft, gentle.
Without.
"Joke." A piece in a lively tempo. A movement of a symphony, sonata, or quartet in quick triple time, replacing the minuet.
Fast.
The written depiction of all the parts of a musical ensemble with the parts stacked vertically and rhythmically aligned.
"Dry." Unornamented.

The second degree of the diatonic scale. Also, the interval formed by a given tone and the next tone above or below it, e.g. c up to d, or c down to b. Intervals of the second may be major, diminished, or augmented.
A division of a musical composition.
"Sign."
Very.
Very soft in the beginning.
A half step. The smallest interval on the keyboard.
Always. Used with other terms, e.g. sempre staccato.
Simple.
Without. Used with other terms, e.g. senza crescendo.
A piece for seven instruments or voices. Seven performers.
The repetition of a melodic pattern on a higher or lower pitch level.
A love song or piece, usually performed below someone's window in the evening. Sereno - Serene, peaceful.

The seventh degree of the diatonic scale. Also, the interval formed by a given tone and the seventh tone above or below it, e.g. c up to b, or c down to d. Intervals of the seventh may be major, minor, diminished, or augmented.

When a seventh (above the root) is added to a triad (root, third, fifth), the result is a seventh chord, e.g. the dominant triad in the key of C major, g-b-d, with the added seventh becomes g-b-d-f and is labelled V'.
Sudden strong accent on a note or chord.
An individually printed song, most often for voice, piano, guitar, or a combination of the three. Any printed music.
The changing of meter within a composition. Synonymous with changing meter.
An indication to continue in the same manner.
Until.
Left hand.
Until.
four chord - The second inversion of a triad, made by placing the fifth of the chord in the lowest voice, e.g. C is g-c-e.
A note/rest half the length of an eighth note and a sixteenth the length of a whole note.

The sixth degree of the diatonic scale. Also, the interval formed by a given tone and the sixth tone above or below it, e.g. c up to a, or c down to e. Intervals of the sixth may be major, minor, diminished, or augmented.
The first inversion of a triad, made by placing the third of the chord in the lowest voice, e.g. c is e-g-c.
Melodic movement of more than one whole step.
Fading away.
Sweet, mild.
Dreamily.
In solmization, the fifth degree of the major scale.
The term for the use of syllables for the degrees of the major scale: do, re, mi, fa, sol, la ti, do. The minor scale (natural) is la, ti, do, re, mi, fa, sol, la.
To perform alone or as the predominant part.
An instrumental piece, often in several movements.
A short sonata.
Sustaining of tone or slackening of tempo.
On string instruments, a bowing technique wherein the bow is bounced on the string at moderate speed.
The most frequently used staff has five horizontal lines, with four spaces, upon which the notes and other musical symbols are placed.
A selection of a song, two or more lines long, characterized by a common meter, rhyme, and number of lines.
Same.
Instruments with strings that produce sound when plucked, bowed, or struck.
A term used to describe a song in which all the stanzas of the text are sung to the same music. The opposite of through-composed.
The fourth degree of the major or minor scale. Also, the name of the triad built on the fourth degree of the scale, indicated by IV in a major key and by iv in a minor key.
Suddenly.
The sixth degree of a major or minor scale. Also, the name of the triad built on the sixth degree of the scale, indicated by VI in a major key and by vi in a minor key.
On the.
The second degree of the major or minor scale. Also, the name of the triad built on the second degree of the scale, indicated by II in a major scale and ii in a minor scale.
On, over.
The use of a nonharmonic tone to delay the resolution of a chord, frequently as it occurs in a cadence.
Quick, light.
A piece for large orchestra, usually in four movements, in which the first movement often is in sonata form. A large orchestra.
Much, so much.
Return to the original tempo.
Tenderly.
The C clef falling on the fourth line of the staff.
Hold or sustain a note longer than the indicated value, usually not as long a duration as the fermata.
Three-part form in which the middle section is different from the other sections. Indicated by ABA.
The Baroque style of using sudden changes in dynamic levels, as opposed to gradual increase and decrease in volume.
A term used to describe music based on chords arranged in intervals of thirds.
The general pitch range of a vocal part.
The term used to describe the way in which melodic lines are combined, either with or without accompaniment. Types include monophonic, homophonic, and polyphonic, or contrapuntal.
A statement of musical subject followed by restatements in different guises.
The study of how music is put together.

The third degree of the diatonic scale. Also, the interval formed by a given tone and the third tone above or below it, e.g. c up to e, or c down to a. Intervals of the third may be major, minor, diminished, or augmented.
composed - A term used to describe a song in which the music for each stanza is different. The opposite of strophic.
In solmization, the seventh degree of the major scale. Also called the leading tone.
The term used to describe the organization of the melodic and harmonic elements to give a feeling of a key center or a tonic pitch.
A note; the basis of music.
The simultaneous sounding of two or more adjacent tones.
On wind instruments, articulation with the tongue.
The first note of a key. Also, the name of the chord built on the first degree of the scale, indicated by I in a major key or i in a minor key.
Tone, key, pitch.
Quick.
Tranquilly; quietly; calm.
Three. Used with other terms, e.g. a tre voci, in three parts.
A chord of three tones arranged in thirds, e.g. the C-major triad c-e-g, root-third-fifth.
A musical ornament performed by the rapid alternation of a given note with a major or minor second above.
Meter based on three beats, or a multiple of three, in a measure.
A group of three notes performed in the time of two of the same kind.
Too much. Used with other terms, e.g. allegro non troppo, not too fast.
All. A direction for the entire ensemble to sing or play simultaneously.

The row may be used in its original form, its inversion, in retrograde, and in the inversion of the retrograde. The system was devised by Arnold Schoenberg in the early 20th century.
Soft pedal.

A little. Used with other words, e.g. un peu piano.
A little.
Repeated fluctuation of pitch.
A brilliant, skillful performer.
Lively, bright.
Turn [the page] quickly.
A note/rest equal to two half notes and four quarter notes.
Instruments in which sound is produced by the vibration of air, including brass and woodwind instruments.
Instruments, originally made of wood, in which sound is produced by the vibration of air, including recorders, flutes, clarinets, saxophones, oboes, and bassoons.
A seven-note diatonic scale with the pattern: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. The most common scale in Western music, creating a bright, happy sound.
terms.example: C major: C-D-E-F-G-A-B-C. Intervals: 1-2-3-4-5-6-7

terms.definition: A seven-note diatonic scale with the pattern: whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole. The relative minor of the major scale, creating a darker, more melancholic sound.
terms.example: A natural minor: A-B-C-D-E-F-G-A. Intervals: 1-2-b3-4-5-b6-b7

terms.definition: A minor scale with a raised seventh degree. Creates a stronger pull to the tonic and is used frequently in classical and jazz music.
terms.example: A harmonic minor: A-B-C-D-E-F-G#-A. Intervals: 1-2-b3-4-5-b6-7

terms.definition: A minor scale that is different ascending (raised 6th and 7th) and descending (natural minor). Used in classical music for smooth melodic lines.
terms.example: A melodic minor ascending: A-B-C-D-E-F#-G#-A. Descending: A-G-F-E-D-C-B-A

terms.definition: A mode starting on the second degree of the major scale. Pattern: whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half, whole. Has a minor feel with a raised sixth.
terms.example: D Dorian: D-E-F-G-A-B-C-D (uses C major key signature). Common in jazz and folk music.

terms.definition: A mode starting on the third degree of the major scale. Pattern: half, whole, whole, whole, half, whole, whole. Has a Spanish, exotic character.
terms.example: E Phrygian: E-F-G-A-B-C-D-E (uses C major key signature)

terms.definition: A mode starting on the fourth degree of the major scale. Pattern: whole, whole, whole, half, whole, whole, half. Has a bright, dreamy quality with a raised fourth.
terms.example: F Lydian: F-G-A-B-C-D-E-F (uses C major key signature)

terms.definition: A mode starting on the fifth degree of the major scale. Pattern: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole. Has a major feel with a lowered seventh, common in folk and rock music.
terms.example: G Mixolydian: G-A-B-C-D-E-F-G (uses C major key signature)

terms.definition: A mode starting on the seventh degree of the major scale. Pattern: half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole. The least stable mode due to its diminished fifth.
terms.example: B Locrian: B-C-D-E-F-G-A-B (uses C major key signature)

terms.definition: A five-note scale using scale degrees 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 of the major scale. Found in many world music traditions, creates an open, pleasant sound.
terms.example: C major pentatonic: C-D-E-G-A

terms.definition: A five-note scale using scale degrees 1, b3, 4, 5, b7 of the natural minor scale. Essential in blues, rock, and jazz.
terms.example: A minor pentatonic: A-C-D-E-G

terms.definition: A six-note scale derived from the minor pentatonic with an added 'blue note' (flatted fifth). The foundation of blues and many jazz styles.
terms.example: A blues scale: A-C-D-Eb-E-G-A

terms.definition: A six-note scale where each note is a whole step apart. Creates an ambiguous, dreamy sound, used by Debussy and in jazz.
terms.example: C whole tone: C-D-E-F#-G#-A#-C

terms.definition: An eight-note scale alternating whole and half steps. Creates tension and is common in jazz and modern classical music.
terms.example: C diminished (whole-half): C-D-Eb-F-Gb-Ab-A-B-C

terms.definition: A three-note chord consisting of a root, major third, and perfect fifth. The most stable and consonant chord, sounds bright and happy.
terms.example: C major: C-E-G. Intervals: root, major 3rd, perfect 5th

terms.definition: A three-note chord consisting of a root, minor third, and perfect fifth. Sounds darker and more melancholic than major.
terms.example: C minor: C-Eb-G. Intervals: root, minor 3rd, perfect 5th

terms.definition: A three-note chord with a minor third and diminished fifth. Sounds tense and unstable, creates strong resolution needs.
terms.example: C diminished: C-Eb-Gb. Intervals: root, minor 3rd, diminished 5th

terms.definition: A three-note chord with a major third and augmented fifth. Sounds bright but unstable, creates ambiguity.
terms.example: C augmented: C-E-G#. Intervals: root, major 3rd, augmented 5th

terms.definition: A major triad with a major seventh. Sounds rich and stable, common in jazz and contemporary music.
terms.example: Cmaj7: C-E-G-B. Intervals: root, major 3rd, perfect 5th, major 7th

terms.definition: A minor triad with a minor seventh. The most common seventh chord in jazz, sounds smooth and mellow.
terms.example: Cm7: C-Eb-G-Bb. Intervals: root, minor 3rd, perfect 5th, minor 7th

terms.definition: A major triad with a minor seventh. Creates strong tension that resolves to the tonic, the most important chord in functional harmony.
terms.example: C7: C-E-G-Bb. Intervals: root, major 3rd, perfect 5th, minor 7th

terms.definition: A diminished triad with a diminished seventh. Highly unstable, can resolve to multiple keys, creates dramatic tension.
terms.example: Cdim7: C-Eb-Gb-A. Intervals: root, minor 3rd, diminished 5th, diminished 7th

terms.definition: A diminished triad with a minor seventh. Common as the leading tone chord in minor keys.
terms.example: Cm7b5: C-Eb-Gb-Bb. Intervals: root, minor 3rd, diminished 5th, minor 7th

terms.definition: A chord where the third is replaced by the fourth. Creates an open, unresolved sound that typically resolves to the major triad.
terms.example: Csus4: C-F-G. Resolves to C major (C-E-G)

terms.definition: A chord where the third is replaced by the second. Creates a gentle, open sound.
terms.example: Csus2: C-D-G

terms.definition: An extended chord adding a ninth above the root. Common in jazz, adds color and richness.
terms.example: C9: C-E-G-Bb-D. Can be major 9th (Cmaj9) or dominant 9th (C9)

terms.definition: An extended chord adding an eleventh above the root. Creates a complex, modern sound.
terms.example: Cm11: C-Eb-G-Bb-D-F

terms.definition: An extended chord adding a thirteenth above the root. The fullest extension, common in jazz.
terms.example: Cmaj13: C-E-G-B-D-F#-A

terms.definition: A triad with an added ninth, without the seventh. Creates a modern, open sound.
terms.example: Cadd9: C-E-G-D

terms.definition: A two-note chord consisting of root and fifth (no third). Common in rock and metal, creates a strong, neutral sound.
terms.example: C5: C-G

terms.definition: Two notes of the same pitch. The most consonant interval, creates complete unity.
terms.example: C to C

terms.definition: A semitone interval. Highly dissonant, creates tension. Also called a half step.
terms.example: C to Db (1 semitone)

terms.definition: A whole tone interval. Slightly dissonant, common in melodies. Also called a whole step.
terms.example: C to D (2 semitones)

terms.definition: A three-semitone interval. Consonant, forms the basis of minor triads.
terms.example: C to Eb (3 semitones)

terms.definition: A four-semitone interval. Very consonant, forms the basis of major triads.
terms.example: C to E (4 semitones)

terms.definition: A five-semitone interval. Consonant and stable, common in harmony.
terms.example: C to F (5 semitones)

terms.definition: An augmented fourth or diminished fifth (6 semitones). The 'devil's interval' - highly dissonant and unstable.
terms.example: C to F# or C to Gb (6 semitones)

terms.definition: A seven-semitone interval. The most consonant interval after the octave, forms the basis of power chords.
terms.example: C to G (7 semitones)

terms.definition: An eight-semitone interval. Consonant, creates a gentle, expressive sound.
terms.example: C to Ab (8 semitones)

terms.definition: A nine-semitone interval. Very consonant, common in melodies and harmony.
terms.example: C to A (9 semitones)

terms.definition: A ten-semitone interval. Slightly dissonant, essential in seventh chords.
terms.example: C to Bb (10 semitones)

terms.definition: An eleven-semitone interval. Dissonant but stable, creates rich color in chords.
terms.example: C to B (11 semitones)

terms.definition: A twelve-semitone interval. The most consonant interval, notes sound like the same pitch at different registers.
terms.example: C to C (12 semitones)

terms.definition: The role of the I chord (tonic) as the home, stable center of a key. All harmony resolves to or from the tonic.
terms.example: In C major, C major chord is the tonic

terms.definition: The role of the V chord (dominant) as creating tension that resolves to the tonic. The strongest harmonic function.
terms.example: In C major, G major (or G7) is the dominant

terms.definition: The role of the IV chord (subdominant) as providing contrast to the tonic, often leading to the dominant.
terms.example: In C major, F major is the subdominant

terms.definition: A system of labeling chords by their scale degree using Roman numerals. Uppercase for major, lowercase for minor.
terms.example: I-vi-IV-V in C major = C-Am-F-G

terms.definition: A dominant chord of a chord other than the tonic. Creates temporary key changes and adds harmonic color.
terms.example: V/V (D7) in C major, resolving to G (the V chord)

terms.definition: Temporarily treating a non-tonic chord as if it were the tonic, often through use of secondary dominants.
terms.example: Using D7-G to temporarily make G feel like the tonic

terms.definition: The movement of individual melodic lines (voices) in harmony. Good voice leading creates smooth, logical chord progressions.
terms.example: Moving from C major to F major with minimal voice movement: C-E-G to C-F-A

terms.definition: A sequence of chords that forms the harmonic foundation of a piece. Common progressions create familiar musical patterns.
terms.example: I-V-vi-IV (C-G-Am-F) is a very common pop progression

terms.definition: A harmonic progression that creates a sense of resolution or pause. Marks the end of phrases or sections.
terms.example: Perfect authentic cadence: V-I (G-C in C major)

terms.definition: A major and minor key that share the same key signature but have different tonics. They contain the same notes.
terms.example: C major and A minor are relative keys (no sharps/flats)

terms.definition: A major and minor key that share the same tonic but have different key signatures.
terms.example: C major and C minor are parallel keys

terms.definition: A chord that exists in both the original and new key, used to smoothly transition between keys during modulation.
terms.example: Am (vi in C major, ii in G major) can pivot from C to G
